newsitem.title: INDIA: Eclipse of India's Congress worries rivals.
newsitem.headline: Eclipse of India's Congress worries rivals.

text.p: India's Congress party, given poor ratings in an influential opinion poll, braced for more bad news in a key state election this week as its rivals fretted over the eclipse of the nation's oldest political machine.

Analysts said the decline of the Congress, which suffered its worst-ever defeat in last year's general elections, could further erode the narrowing middle ground in Indian politics, separating the prospering right from the hardening left.

"I am seriously worried for the Congress," said K.R. Malkani, senior ideologue of the rightwing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), the largest single party in the Lok Sabha or lower house of parliament.
"I hope it doesn't disintegrate. The BJP needs the Congress as a rival national party."

A leading opinion poll published by India Today magazine on Sunday predicted that Congress would suffer more losses if Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's coalition government falls and snap elections were held soon.
Based on a survey of 12,832 registered voters, the poll said the BJP, the main opposition party, would add 46 seats to 1996 last year's tally of 194, including allies.

The Congress was expected to drop to a paltry 115 seats from the 139 it holds. Deve Gowda's United Front alliance, reluctantly supported by the Congress in the 545-seat lower house of parliament, would lose nine seats, the poll said.

"We have been trying to roll back the Congress, so it has weakened. But it would be wrong to write it off completely," said Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M) politburo member Prakash Karat. "In order to roll it back we do not want a more reactionary party, like the BJP to take its place."
Analysts said Karat's remarks implied that the CPI-M needed the Congress weak but intact.
Deve Gowda's eight-month-old minority government, with fewer than 200 deputies, is accused by the BJP and the Congress of mismanaging foreign policy and neglecting the economy.

There is growing speculation that Congress President Sitaram Kesri, who succeeded former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao after a spate of corruption charges forced Rao to quit in September, wants to pull out of the alliance with Deve Gowda.
Publicly the Congress has maintained it has no plans to bring down Deve Gowda's government during the budget session of parliament which is scheduled to start on February 20.
The Congress had more reasons this week to hold back from any move to topple Deve Gowda.
Analysts said the party was headed for losses, even defeat, in the assembly elections on Friday in the rich agricultural and politically crucial northern state of Punjab.

The India Today poll, which said 62 percent of the respondents wanted Deve Gowda replaced by someone else, also said Kesri received poor marks as a possible replacement, with only two percent backing his candidature.

In a telling comment on the state of the Congress, the India Today poll said Sonia Gandhi, the widow of former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, was the third most favoured person after the BJP's Atal Behari Vajpayee and Deve Gowda when respondents were asked "Who do you think would make India's best Prime Minister?"
Sonia Gandhi, who has never held public office, is widely acknowledged to wield considerable influence even after the demise of the Nehru-Gandhi family dynasty.

The Congress, which spearheaded the drive for independence from British rule, has ruled the country for most of the past half-century. But it is now a shadow of its former self and controls only nine, mainly insignificant states of India's 25.
Its weaknesses have not diluted the party's hope of a miraculous revival.
"We expect the government to fall under its own contradictions," Congress spokesman Ved Prakash told Reuters.
"If elections are held in the next six months, the Congress will bounce back. But we are not planning to do anything drastic at the moment," Prakash said.
